medication-management-caregiver.title: Helping Your Loved One Stay Safe with Medicines
medication-management-caregiver.subtitle: A guide for family caregivers to manage medications safely and be a key partner in healthcare.

item-1.trigger: Why Older Adults Need Extra Help
item-1.cardTitle: Your Loved One's Most Important Safety Net

content.p1: As people age, they often develop more health conditions and need more medicines. Taking many medications (polypharmacy) increases the chance of problems.
content.li1: About 1 in 5 people over 70 takes five or more different medicines.
content.li2: The body handles medicines differently with age, making side effects more likely.
content.li3: A medication problem can be a major reason for a hospital admission.

content.p1: A bad reaction to a medicine in an older person might not be what you expect. It often looks like a sudden change in their overall condition. Never dismiss these signs as "just getting old."
content.li1: Sudden confusion, memory problems, or acting strangely (delirium).
content.li2: More falls, or new dizziness and unsteadiness.
content.li3: New or worsening bladder or bowel control issues.
content.li4: Unusual sleepiness or being hard to wake up.
content.li5: Sudden loss of appetite or feeling very tired.
content.li6: A new depressed mood or loss of interest in things.
content.p2: Always consider that a new symptom might be a medication side effect and call the doctor.

content.p1: Sometimes, a side effect from Drug #1 is mistaken for a new health problem. The doctor might then prescribe Drug #2 to treat that side effect. This can lead to even more problems. This is called the prescribing cascade.
content.p2: A blood pressure pill (Drug #1) causes swollen ankles. The doctor sees the swelling and prescribes a water pill (Drug #2) to fix it. The water pill can then cause dizziness, leading to a fall.
content.p3: You can help stop this by telling the doctor about any new symptom that appears after a medicine is started or changed.

item-4.trigger: Your Action Plan for Medication Safety

content.li1: Keep an "All-Meds" Master List: Maintain one updated list of every prescription, over-the-counter item, vitamin, and supplement. Note the name, dose, and reason for each. Bring this list to EVERY appointment.
content.li2: Use One Pharmacy: Fill all prescriptions at the same pharmacy. This allows the pharmacist to spot dangerous interactions.
content.li3: Use a Pill Organizer: A weekly pill box helps prevent missed or double doses.
content.li4: Ask Questions at Discharge: Leaving the hospital is high-risk. Go over the final medication list with the nurse or doctor and ask: "What is each new medicine for?", "Which medicines should be stopped?", and "Who do I call if I have a problem?".

alzheimers-caregiver.title: A Detailed Caregiver's Guide to Understanding Alzheimer's Disease
alzheimers-caregiver.subtitle: This guide provides families with in-depth information to understand what Alzheimer's is, how it progresses, how it is diagnosed, and how to recognize and manage the challenging behavioral changes that are part of the disease.

content.p1: Alzheimer's is a physical disease that causes a slow decline in memory, thinking, and reasoning skills. It is not a normal part of aging. It is the most common cause of dementia.
content.p3: To understand Alzheimer's, it helps to picture the brain as a massive, busy network of communication lines. The disease creates two types of "roadblocks" that disrupt this communication:
content.li1: Plaques: These are sticky clumps that build up between the brain cells.
content.li2: Tangles: These are twisted fibers that build up inside the brain cells.
content.p4: Over many years, these plaques and tangles damage and kill brain cells, causing the brain to shrink and leading to the symptoms we see. This process actually starts long before any memory problems are noticeable.

item-2.title: 2.1 Things We Can and Can't Change

content.p1: Things We Can't Change
content.p2: Some risk factors are simply part of who we are. It's important to remember that having a risk factor does not mean a person will get the disease.
content.li1: Age: This is the single biggest risk factor. The older a person gets, the higher their risk.
content.li2: Genetics: While rare, directly inherited forms exist. For most people, a gene called ApoE4 can increase the risk, but many people with this gene never get Alzheimer's, and many who get Alzheimer's don't have this gene.
content.p4: Research shows that a healthy lifestyle can help protect the brain. You can play a huge role in encouraging these habits. The seven most important areas to focus on are:
content.li3: Staying physically active.
content.li4: Managing blood pressure and diabetes, especially in middle age.
content.li9: Eating a healthy diet with plenty of fish, fruits, and vegetables.

content.p1: Alzheimer's progresses along a continuum. Recognizing these stages can help you understand the changes you are seeing.
content.h4_1: The Earliest Sign: Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD)
content.p2: This is when a person starts to notice their own memory is slipping, but their performance on memory tests is still normal. It can be caused by many things, like stress, but it's important to mention it to the doctor.
content.p3: MCI is diagnosed when memory or thinking problems are noticeable to others and can be measured on tests, but the person is still able to manage their everyday life independently. They may need help with complex tasks like managing finances, but they can still handle their basic personal care.
content.p4: Dementia is diagnosed when the thinking and memory problems have become severe enough to interfere with a person's ability to live safely and independently. This stage is often broken down into:
content.li1: Mild: The person needs help with some daily tasks (like paying bills or remembering appointments) but can still manage many things on their own.
content.li2: Moderate: The person needs more help with basic tasks like dressing and grooming. Confusion worsens, and personality changes may become more pronounced.
content.li3: Severe: The person requires full-time, hands-on care for all their basic needs.

item-4.trigger: Chapter 4: How a Diagnosis is Made
item-4.title: 4.1 Your Role and What to Expect

content.p1: Your Role as the Expert Observer
content.p2: There is no single, simple test for Alzheimer's. The doctor will act like a detective, putting together clues from many sources. You are the most important source of clues. Your description of the changes you've seen in your loved one over time is critical to the diagnosis.
content.p3: What to Expect at the Appointment
content.li1: A Detailed Conversation: The doctor will ask about what symptoms you've noticed, when they started, and how they affect daily life.
content.li2: Memory and Thinking Tests: The doctor will do some brief tests in the office, like the "five-word test" or the "Mini-Mental State Exam" (MMSE) to get a snapshot of their cognitive function. They may also refer your loved one to a neuropsychologist for more detailed testing.
content.li3: Brain Scans (CT or MRI): A brain scan is a standard part of the workup. Its purpose is twofold:
content.li3_sub1: To rule out other problems that can cause memory loss, like a stroke, brain tumor, or fluid on the brain.
content.li3_sub2: To look for signs of brain shrinkage, especially in the memory centers (the hippocampus), which is a hallmark of AD.
content.li4: Other Advanced Tests: In some cases, especially when the diagnosis is unclear, the doctor may suggest a spinal tap (lumbar puncture) to look for the plaque and tangle proteins in the spinal fluid, or a special PET scan to see amyloid plaques in the brain.

item-5.title: 5.1 Why Behaviors Change and What to Look For

content.p1: Why Do Behaviors Change?
content.p2: The damage to the brain from Alzheimer's can cause changes in personality, mood, and behavior. It is crucial to remember that these behaviors are a symptom of the disease, not a willful act.
content.p3: Common Behaviors in the Early and Moderate Stages
content.p4: The most common behavioral changes are often subtle at first. You might notice:
content.li1: Apathy: A loss of motivation and interest in activities they used to enjoy.
content.li2: Anxiety: Feeling worried, restless, or on edge.
content.li3: Depression (Dysphoria): Feeling sad, tearful, or hopeless.
content.li4: Irritability: Being easily annoyed or having a "short fuse."
content.li5: Agitation: Restlessness, pacing, or an inability to sit still.
content.p5: When you see the doctor, they may use a questionnaire called the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI). This is not a test for your loved one, but a structured way for the doctor to ask you about these behaviors. It helps them understand the severity of the symptoms and the amount of stress it is causing you as the caregiver, which is a very important part of the care plan.

fall-prevention.title: Staying Steady and Safe: A Guide to Fall Prevention
fall-prevention.subtitle: This module is designed to empower older adults and their caregivers with the knowledge and tools to prevent falls and maintain independence.

item-1.title: Why falls happen more as we age

content.p1: As we get older, our bodies change. Common age-related changes like decreased vision, shifts in balance and muscle strength, and side effects from medications can make falls more likely.
content.li1: Medical Conditions: Diagnoses like arthritis, osteoporosis, diabetes, or neurological disorders (e.g., Parkinson's disease) can affect your stability.
content.li2: Medication Review: Certain medications, especially when taken together, can cause dizziness or drowsiness. It's vital to have a doctor or pharmacist review all your current medications regularly.
content.li3: Previous Falls: If you've fallen in the past year, your risk of falling again is higher. This is often because the factors that caused the first fall are still present.
content.li4: Sensory Changes: Changes in vision and hearing can significantly impact your balance and coordination.

item-2.title: Practical steps for a safer home

content.li1: Clear the Clutter: Keep walkways clear of electrical cords, throw rugs, and other obstacles that could cause tripping.
content.li2: Improve Lighting: Add nightlights in hallways, bathrooms, and bedrooms. Make sure light switches are easy to reach.
content.li3: Bathroom Safety: Install grab bars in the shower and next to the toilet. Use non-slip mats and consider a shower chair for added stability.
content.li4: Stairway Safety: Ensure handrails are on both sides of the stairs and that stairways are always well-lit.
content.li5: Kitchen Safety: Arrange frequently used items on lower shelves to avoid using a step stool. Clean up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.

item-3.title: Maintaining strength and balance through exercise

content.li1: Strength and Balance Exercises: Simple exercises like chair yoga, tai chi, or leg lifts can improve leg strength and balance. Look for local classes or online videos designed for seniors.
content.li2: Walking Aids: If you use a cane or walker, make sure it is the correct height and that the rubber tips are not worn down. A physical therapist can help fit it properly.
content.li3: Appropriate Footwear: Wear supportive, non-slip shoes both inside and outside the home. Avoid walking in socks or flimsy slippers.

content.li1: Vitamin D and Calcium: These are essential for strong bones. Get them from dairy products, fortified foods, and supplements if recommended by your doctor.
content.li2: Stay Hydrated: Dehydration can cause dizziness and confusion. Drink plenty of water throughout the day.
content.li3: Regular Meals: Don't skip meals. This helps prevent drops in blood sugar that can lead to lightheadedness and instability.

item-5.trigger: What to Do If You Fall
item-5.title: Having a plan of action

content.li1: How to Get Up Safely: Stay still for a moment to assess for injuries. If you feel you can get up, roll onto your hands and knees, crawl to a sturdy chair, and use it to help you stand.
content.li2: When to Call for Help: If you are hurt or cannot get up, call for help. Use a medical alert device, a phone, or call out for assistance.
content.li3: Emergency Plan: Consider a medical alert device, especially if you live alone. Keep a phone within reach at all times, and have emergency numbers posted in a visible place.

parkinsonism-care-professional.title: A Comprehensive Nursing Guide to Parkinson's Disease in the Older Adult
parkinsonism-care-professional.subtitle: A detailed clinical framework for the assessment, diagnosis, and complex management of Parkinson's Disease in geriatric patients.

item-1.trigger: Chapter 1: The Foundations of Parkinson's Disease in Geriatrics
item-1.title: 1.1 Pathophysiology and Epidemiology

content.p1: Parkinson's Disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. Its key pathological hallmarks are a loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the presence of Lewy Bodies (accumulations of α-synuclein).
content.li1: Prevalence: Affects approximately 1% of individuals over age 65.
content.li2: Late-Onset: Most patients in geriatric settings have long-standing disease and present with advanced complications.
content.li3: Established Factors: A family history of PD is found in 6-10% of cases.
content.li4: Weak Associations: Rural living, exposure to pesticides/herbicides, and head injuries.
content.li5: Protective Factors: Cigarette smoking and coffee consumption appear to be protective.

item-2.trigger: Chapter 2: Clinical Assessment: A Multifaceted Approach
item-2.title: 2.1 Clinical Assessment

content.p1: PD signs are typically asymmetric at onset. Assess for:
content.li1: Rest Tremor: 4–6 Hz frequency, most prominent at rest.
content.li2: Bradykinesia/Akinesia: Poverty of movement, loss of facial expression ("masked facies").
content.li3: Rigidity: "Lead-pipe" type of increased muscle tone on passive movement.
content.li4: Postural Instability: Occurs later and is a primary cause of falls.
content.li5: Gait and Posture: Abnormal flexed posture, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing.
content.li6: Freezing of Gait: A feeling of feet being "glued to the floor."
content.p2: Autonomic Dysfunction: Orthostatic hypotension, constipation, sialorrhea, urinary urgency.
content.p3: Neuropsychiatric Symptoms: Depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment. Note: Dementia is never an early sign of idiopathic PD.

item-3.trigger: Chapter 3: Differential Diagnosis in the Older Adult
item-3.title: 3.1 Differential Diagnosis

content.p1: Extremely common. Caused by neuroleptics (antipsychotics) and antiemetics (metoclopramide). Signs are usually bilateral and symmetrical with no rest tremor. Prevention is key: avoid neuroleptics in older patients where possible.
content.li1: Lewy Body Dementia (LBD): Dementia occurs within months of or precedes parkinsonism.
content.li2: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP): Early falls, axial rigidity, and limited vertical gaze.
content.li3: Vascular Parkinsonism: Stepwise progression associated with strokes.

content.p1: The main treatment for PD in older adults. "Start low and go slow." Administer 30 mins before meals for best absorption.
content.li1: "Wearing-Off": Return of symptoms before next dose. Manage by increasing dosing frequency or adding COMT-inhibitor.
content.li2: Dyskinesias: Involuntary movements at peak dose. Amantadine can help.
content.li3: Psychiatric Side Effects: Hallucinations/delirium. Clozapine and Pimavanserin are effective treatments.
content.li4: Dopamine Agonists: High risk of severe psychiatric side effects in older adults.
content.li5: Anticholinergic Drugs: Never used in older people with PD due to high risk of delirium.

content.p1: Management extends far beyond medication. Therapy sessions should be timed with the peak effect of L-dopa.
content.li1: Physical Therapy: Essential for gait training, balance, posture, and fall prevention.
content.li2: Speech Therapy: Crucial for managing dysarthria (speech) and dysphagia (swallowing).
content.li3: Supportive and Palliative Care: As the disease progresses, focus shifts to managing loss of independence and ensuring quality of life.

dementia-care-professional.title: A Comprehensive Nursing Guide to Delirium in the Older Adult
dementia-care-professional.subtitle: This lesson provides a detailed clinical framework for the assessment, differential diagnosis, and complex management of delirium in geriatric patients.

content.p1: Delirium is a complex and acute neuropsychiatric syndrome, often described as acute brain failure. It represents a final common pathway for many acute illnesses and is characterized by a disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition. Its presentation is highly variable, ranging from hypoactive lethargy to hyperactive agitation.
content.p2: Delirium is a medical emergency associated with significant morbidity, mortality, and cost. It can accelerate cognitive decline, increase the risk of institutionalization, and lead to poorer functional outcomes.
content.p3: Recognizing motor subtypes (hypoactive, hyperactive, mixed) and clinical phenotypes (Postoperative Delirium, Delirium Superimposed on Dementia) is useful as they may have different etiologies and management strategies.

content.p1: The Systems Integration Failure Hypothesis (SIFH) suggests delirium results from a breakdown in neuronal network connectivity, driven by factors like neuronal aging, neuroinflammation, and neurotransmitter imbalances. This complexity helps explain why single-agent pharmacological treatments have failed.
content.p2: A patient's risk is a function of their baseline vulnerability (predisposing factors like dementia or frailty) and the acute insults they endure (precipitating factors like infection or new medications). Use mnemonics like "DELIRIUM IS VERY PAINFUL" to recall common triggers.

content.p1: The gold standard for diagnosis remains the DSM-5 criteria. Daily screening of all hospitalized older adults is essential for early detection. The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) is the most widely used tool, requiring (1) Acute Onset and Fluctuating Course and (2) Inattention, plus either (3) Disorganized Thinking or (4) Altered Level of Consciousness.

item-4.trigger: Chapter 4: Prevention - The First Line of Defense
item-4.title: Prevention Strategies

content.p1: Up to 40% of delirium cases are preventable through multicomponent, non-pharmacological interventions.
content.li1: Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP): A protocol-driven program targeting six key risk factors: cognitive impairment, sleep deprivation, immobility, vision impairment, hearing impairment, and dehydration.
content.li2: ABCDEF Bundle (for ICU): A mnemonic for a comprehensive bundle of care practices including pain management, early mobility, and family engagement.
content.li3: Avoid High-Risk Medications: Scrutinize the medication list for anticholinergics (diphenhydramine), benzodiazepines, and other psychoactive drugs.
content.li4: Judicious Deprescribing: Taper chronic benzodiazepines or certain antidepressants to avoid withdrawal syndromes that can precipitate delirium.

content.h4_1: Non-Pharmacological Management: The Mainstay of Treatment
content.p1: Once delirium occurs, non-pharmacological measures are the primary treatment. The T-A-DA (Tolerate, Anticipate, Don't Agitate) method is a useful behavioral management approach. This involves tolerating non-dangerous behaviors, anticipating patient needs, and minimizing agitating triggers.
content.h4_2: Pharmacological Management: A Limited and High-Risk Role
content.p2: No agents are approved by the FDA for the treatment of delirium.
content.li1: Benzodiazepines: Should not be used, as they can worsen delirium. The only exceptions are deliria due to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
content.li2: Antipsychotics (e.g., Haloperidol): Have failed to show efficacy in reducing delirium duration or severity. They carry a Black Box warning for increased mortality in patients with dementia. Their use should be reserved only for cases where severe agitation poses an imminent danger, and only after all non-pharmacological methods have failed.

joint-problems-professional.title: Clinical Management of Rheumatic Disorders in Older Adults
joint-problems-professional.subtitle: A review of the assessment and management of common joint diseases like OA, RA, and Gout.

content.p1: Advanced age is the most important risk factor. Cartilage loss is the hallmark pathology, accompanied by synovial inflammation, osteophyte formation, and subchondral bone sclerosis. Other risk factors include obesity, female gender, trauma/joint injury, and quadriceps weakness.
content.p2: Gout is an inflammatory reaction to monosodium urate (MSU) crystals associated with hyperuricemia. Risk factors include age, male gender, renal disease, alcohol use, and diuretic use. Pseudogout is a similar reaction to calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate (CPPD) crystals, with advanced age being the most critical risk factor.
content.p3: Late-onset RA differs from young-onset, with more proximal joint involvement and a more aggressive course. The characteristic pathology is synovial inflammation (pannus formation) that erodes cartilage and bone.

content.li1: Osteoarthritis: Insidious onset, chronic course. Affects DIPs (Heberden nodes), PIPs (Bouchard nodes), hips, knees. X-rays show joint space narrowing and osteophytes. Labs (ANA, RF, ESR) are typically negative.
content.li2: Rheumatoid Arthritis: More acute/subacute onset. Often involves proximal joints. Labs may show positive RF/anti-CCP and elevated ESR/CRP. X-rays can show erosions.
content.li3: Gout: Acute, intermittent attacks. Classically affects the first MTP. Confirmed by negatively birefringent, needle-shaped MSU crystals in synovial fluid.
content.li4: Pseudogout: Acute, intermittent attacks, often affecting the knee or wrist. Confirmed by positively birefringent, rod-shaped CPPD crystals. X-rays may show chondrocalcinosis.
content.li5: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR): Acute onset of pain/stiffness in shoulder and hip girdles. Markedly elevated ESR/CRP. Must screen for Giant-Cell Arteritis (GCA).
content.p1: The Role of Arthrocentesis: Joint fluid analysis is crucial to differentiate inflammatory vs. noninflammatory arthritis and to rule out septic arthritis. A WBC count >2,000 indicates inflammation.

content.li1: First-Line: Topical NSAIDs are preferred over oral due to better safety profile. Acetaminophen can be trialed.
content.li2: Oral NSAIDs: Discouraged due to CV, GI, and renal toxicity. Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration if necessary.
content.li3: Intra-articular Steroids: Can provide moderate short-term pain relief for knee OA.
content.li4: Opioids: Not effective for pain or function and best avoided due to significant adverse effects.
content.li5: Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT): Indicated for ≥2 attacks/year or tophi. Allopurinol is first-line. Goal is serum uric acid ≤6 mg/dL.
content.li6: Prophylaxis: Start low-dose colchicine or steroids when initiating ULT to prevent flares.
content.li7: Acute Flare Management: IA steroids for 1-2 joints. For polyarticular flares, use oral colchicine or a short course of steroids. Avoid NSAIDs in most older adults.
content.li8: First-Line: Early referral to rheumatology for Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs), often triple therapy (e.g., methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine).
content.li9: Biologics: For patients who fail DMARDs. Require screening for TB and hepatitis before initiation.
content.li10: Steroids: Used as a bridge to DMARDs, but not for long-term therapy. Prophylaxis for osteoporosis is critical if used for >3 months.

content.p1: A multimodal, interprofessional approach is critical for managing arthritis in older adults.
content.li1: Education and Goal Setting: Establish realistic goals focused on pain reduction and functional improvement.
content.li2: Physical & Occupational Therapy: Essential for strength training, flexibility, assistive device selection (canes, walkers), and joint protection strategies.
content.li3: Weight Loss: Critically important for overweight/obese patients with OA of the knee or hip.
content.li4: Cardiovascular Risk Management: Crucial for patients with inflammatory arthritis (RA, Gout), as they have a higher risk of CV events.

vision-problems-professional.title: Geriatric Ophthalmology: A Clinical Review
vision-problems-professional.subtitle: A module for PCPs on the diagnosis and management of common age-related eye conditions.

item-1.trigger: The Red Eye: Red Flags and Differential
item-1.title: Urgent vs. Non-Urgent Conditions

content.p1: Most red eye presentations in primary care are benign. The key is to identify red flags that indicate a vision-threatening condition requiring same-day ophthalmology referral.
content.li1: Decreased visual acuity (not resolved with blinking)
content.li2: Significant eye pain (more than irritation or foreign body sensation)
content.li3: Photophobia
content.li4: Ciliary flush (a ring of hyperemia around the limbus)
content.li5: Corneal opacification or epithelial disruption (visible with fluorescein)
content.li7: Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP > 40 mmHg is an emergency)
content.p2: Conditions like blepharitis, dry eye syndrome, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and most cases of conjunctivitis can often be managed initially in the primary care setting. Treatment includes warm compresses, artificial tears, and topical antibiotics if a bacterial cause is strongly suspected.

content.p1: A multifactorial disease causing discomfort, visual disturbance, and tear film instability. Risk factors include advanced age, female sex, Sjögren syndrome, and polypharmacy (especially diuretics, antihistamines, antidepressants). Management focuses on education, environmental modification, artificial tears (preservative-free preferred for frequent use), and addressing underlying conditions like blepharitis.
content.p2: A leading cause of irreversible vision loss. "Dry" (atrophic) AMD is more common, while "wet" (neovascular) AMD causes more severe vision loss. Key risk factors are age, smoking, and genetics. Patients should monitor for metamorphopsia with an Amsler grid. Management for intermediate/advanced AMD includes AREDS2 vitamin supplementation. Wet AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.
content.p3: Lens opacification causing decreased visual acuity, glare, and poor contrast sensitivity. The only treatment is surgical extraction with intraocular lens implantation. The indication for surgery is functional impairment, not a specific VA number. Surgery is highly effective and can improve quality of life, cognition, and reduce fall risk.
content.p4: A progressive optic neuropathy characterized by visual field loss, often asymptomatically until advanced stages. Elevated IOP is the primary modifiable risk factor. Other risks include age, African ethnicity, and family history. Management involves lowering IOP with topical medications (prostaglandin analogues are first-line), laser trabeculoplasty, or surgery.
content.p5: A common microvascular complication of diabetes. Risk factors include duration of DM, poor glycemic control, and hypertension. All patients with DM require annual dilated fundus examinations for screening. Management involves strict control of glucose and blood pressure, with anti-VEGF injections and laser photocoagulation for vision-threatening stages (proliferative DR, macular edema).

content.p1: Systemic absorption of topical eye medications can be significant in older adults. Educate patients on nasolacrimal occlusion (gentle pressure on the inner canthus) or simple eye closure for 1-2 minutes after instillation to minimize absorption.
content.li1: Beta-blockers (e.g., Timolol): Can cause bradycardia, hypotension, and bronchospasm. Use with caution in patients with COPD, asthma, or heart block.
content.li2: Alpha-adrenergic agonists (e.g., Brimonidine): Can cause dry mouth and fatigue.
content.li3: Anticholinergics & Antihistamines: Can exacerbate dry eye and carry a risk of inducing angle-closure glaucoma in predisposed individuals.
content.li4: Corticosteroids: Long-term use can cause cataracts and elevated IOP.

lung-infections-professional.title: Pneumonia in Older Adults: A Clinical Guide
lung-infections-professional.subtitle: A clinical framework for the assessment, triage, and management of pneumonia in geriatric patients.

item-1.trigger: The Geriatric Context: Why Pneumonia is Different
item-1.title: The Geriatric Context

content.p1: In older adults, pneumonia is not just a lung infection; it's a systemic event with high rates of hospitalization and mortality. The risk is elevated due to a confluence of age-related changes and common comorbidities.
content.li1: Impaired Defenses: Reduced cough effectiveness, poor mucociliary clearance, and weakened cellular immunity.
content.li2: Aspiration: Microaspiration of oropharyngeal contents is a frequent cause, exacerbated by neurological diseases (stroke, dementia), dysphagia, GERD, and the use of sedative drugs.
content.li3: Comorbidities: Pre-existing conditions like COPD, heart failure, and diabetes significantly increase susceptibility.

content.p1: The classic presentation of lobar pneumonia is often absent. Your assessment must have a high index of suspicion for atypical signs.
content.p2: Tachypnoea (respiratory rate >30/min) is a more reliable sign than cough. Localized crackles may be faint or absent.
content.p3: Pneumonia frequently manifests as a non-specific decline. Look for:
content.li1: Delirium: An acute change in mental status may be the only presenting sign.
content.li2: Sepsis/Shock: Unexplained hypotension, tachycardia, or hypothermia.
content.li3: New Cardiac Events: Onset of new atrial fibrillation or a heart failure exacerbation.
content.li4: GI Symptoms: Abdominal pain, nausea, or paralytic ileus.

item-3.trigger: Triage and Severity: When to Hospitalize (CRB-65)
item-3.title: Triage with CRB-65

content.p1: The CRB-65 scale is a simple, effective tool for bedside triage to assess the severity and need for hospitalization. One point is given for each of the following:
content.li1: Confusion (new onset)
content.li2: Respiratory Rate (≥30/min)
content.li3: Blood Pressure (Systolic <90 mmHg or Diastolic ≤60 mmHg)
content.p2: Clinical Pearl: Every older patient will have a score of at least 1. A score of 1-2 warrants strong consideration for hospital referral. A score of 3-4 requires urgent admission.

content.p1: Focus on hydration, nutrition, oral care, and prevention of immobility complications (VTE, pressure ulcers).
content.p2: Clinical response at 48 hours is a key decision point. An unfavorable response is a red flag requiring re-evaluation for resistant organisms, complications, or an incorrect initial diagnosis (e.g., PE).
content.li1: Vaccination: Advocate for and administer annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
content.li2: Aspiration Prevention: Screen for swallowing disorders, implement precautions, and advocate for reducing unnecessary sedative medications.
